title: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: The oxidation state of cobalt in $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3$ is:
questions.solution:
Ammonia is a **neutral** ligand and there are three chloride counter-ions outside the coordination sphere, each $-1$.

So the complex ion is $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, and since the ligands contribute nothing:

$x + 6(0) = +3 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+3}$.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: In an octahedral field, the $d$ orbitals split into:
questions.solution:
In an **octahedral** field the ligands approach along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes.

The $e_g$ orbitals ($d_{z^{2}}$ and $d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}$) point **directly at** the ligands, so they are repelled more and rise in energy. The $t_{2g}$ orbitals ($d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{zx}$) point **between** the ligands and fall.

So $t_{2g}$ is lower and $e_g$ higher, separated by $\Delta_o$.

In a **tetrahedral** field the arrangement is reversed, and $\Delta_t \approx \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ — which is why tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: Which ligand is a **strong field** ligand?
questions.solution:
The spectrochemical series runs, in part:

$\text{I}^{-} < \text{Br}^{-} < \text{Cl}^{-} < \text{F}^{-} < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{en} < \text{NO}_2^{-} < \mathbf{\text{CN}^{-}} < \text{CO}$

**Cyanide** is near the strong-field end. It produces a large $\Delta_o$, so electrons pair up in $t_{2g}$ rather than occupy $e_g$, giving a **low-spin** complex.

The series is largely empirical, and its ordering is only partly explained by electrostatics — pi-acceptor ligands such as $\text{CN}^{-}$ and $\text{CO}$ rank far higher than charge alone would suggest.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.solution:
A colligative property depends on the **number** of solute particles and not on what they are.

The four are: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and **osmotic pressure**.

Osmotic pressure is the most sensitive of them, which is why it is used to find the molar masses of polymers and proteins where the others are too small to measure.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: The number of atoms per unit cell in a face-centred cubic lattice is:
questions.solution:
Corners: $8 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 1$ (each corner atom is shared by eight cells).

Faces: $6 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 3$ (each face atom is shared by two cells).

Total $= 1 + 3 = \mathbf{4}$ atoms.

For comparison, simple cubic has 1 and body-centred cubic has 2. FCC packing efficiency is $74\%$, the highest possible for equal spheres.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.solution:
This is a square planar $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ complex, which shows **geometrical** isomerism: the two chlorides may sit adjacent (**cis**) or opposite (**trans**).

The distinction is not academic. **Cisplatin**, the cis isomer, is a widely used anticancer drug, while the trans isomer is therapeutically inactive — because only the cis arrangement can bind to two adjacent guanine bases on DNA.

Square planar complexes are not optically active, since the molecular plane is a plane of symmetry.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: The van't Hoff factor $i$ for $\text{NaCl}$ assuming complete dissociation is:
questions.solution:
$\text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$ gives **two** particles from one formula unit, so $i = \mathbf{2}$.

$\text{CaCl}_2$ gives $i = 3$ and $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ gives $i = 5$.

In real solutions $i$ is slightly **less** than the ideal value because of ion pairing, and it can be **less than 1** for solutes that associate, such as benzoic acid in benzene, which dimerises.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: A **Schottky** defect in an ionic crystal involves:
options: An ion moving to an interstitial site
Equal numbers of cations and anions missing
questions.solution:
A **Schottky** defect is a pair of vacancies — one cation and one anion missing together, preserving electrical neutrality. It **decreases the density** of the crystal.

A **Frenkel** defect is an ion displaced into an interstitial site, so nothing leaves the crystal and the **density is unchanged**.

Schottky defects are favoured when the ions are of similar size, as in $\text{NaCl}$; Frenkel defects when there is a large size difference, as in $\text{AgBr}$, where the small $\text{Ag}^{+}$ can fit interstitially.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: The coordination number of the central metal in $[\text{Cu}(\text{en})_2]^{2+}$, where en is ethylenediamine, is:
questions.solution:
Ethylenediamine is **bidentate** — it donates through both of its nitrogen atoms.

Two such ligands give $2 \times 2 = \mathbf{4}$ donor atoms, so the coordination number is 4, not 2.

Coordination number counts **donor atoms**, never ligand molecules. Chelating ligands like this form unusually stable complexes, an entropy-driven effect known as the chelate effect.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: Find the boiling point elevation, in kelvin, of a $0.5\ \text{molal}$ aqueous solution of glucose. Take $K_b = 0.52\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$.
questions.solution:
Glucose is a non-electrolyte, so $i = 1$.

$\Delta T_b = iK_bm = 1 \times 0.52 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{0.26\ \text{K}}$.

The solution boils at $100.26^\circ\text{C}$.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: How many unpaired electrons are there in the low-spin octahedral complex $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}$? (Fe is $+2$, $d^{6}$.)
questions.solution:
Iron(II) is $d^{6}$, and cyanide is a **strong field** ligand, so $\Delta_o$ is large and the complex is **low spin**.

All six electrons therefore pair up in the three lower $t_{2g}$ orbitals rather than occupying the higher $e_g$ set:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$

Unpaired electrons $= \mathbf{0}$, so the complex is **diamagnetic**.

With a weak-field ligand such as water the same $d^{6}$ ion would be high spin, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$, with **four** unpaired electrons and paramagnetic — the same metal in the same oxidation state behaving quite differently.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: How many atoms are there per unit cell in a body-centred cubic lattice?
questions.solution:
Corners: $8 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 1$.

Body centre: $1 \times 1 = 1$ (it lies wholly within the cell and is shared with nothing).

Total $= \mathbf{2}$ atoms per unit cell.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: Find the osmotic pressure, in atmospheres, of a $0.1\ \text{M}$ glucose solution at $300\ \text{K}$. Take $R = 0.082\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. Give the answer to two decimal places.

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: What is the oxidation state of iron in $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$?
questions.solution:
Potassium is $+1$ each and cyanide is $-1$ each. Let iron be $x$.

$4(+1) + x + 6(-1) = 0$

$4 + x - 6 = 0$

$x = \mathbf{+2}$

questions.chapter: Coordination Compounds, Solutions and the Solid State
questions.q: Explain crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes. Define the spectrochemical series, and use crystal field theory to explain why $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is paramagnetic while $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}$ is diamagnetic, although the iron is $+2$ in both. Explain also why transition metal complexes are coloured.
questions.solution:
**The splitting.** In a free metal ion the five $d$ orbitals are **degenerate**, all of the same energy.

Bring six ligands up along the $\pm x$, $\pm y$ and $\pm z$ axes, as in an octahedral complex, and their lone pairs repel the $d$ electrons. But not equally, because the orbitals are not all pointing the same way:

- $d_{z^{2}}$ and $d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}$ point **directly along the axes, straight at the ligands**. They are repelled strongly and are **raised** in energy. This pair is labelled $e_g$.
- $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$ and $d_{zx}$ point **between** the axes, away from the ligands. They are repelled less and are **lowered**. This set of three is labelled $t_{2g}$.

The energy gap between them is the **crystal field splitting energy, $\Delta_o$**. The centre of gravity is preserved: each $e_g$ orbital rises by $0.6\Delta_o$ and each $t_{2g}$ orbital falls by $0.4\Delta_o$.

**The spectrochemical series** is the experimental ordering of ligands by the size of $\Delta_o$ they produce:

$\text{I}^{-} < \text{Br}^{-} < \text{Cl}^{-} < \text{F}^{-} < \text{OH}^{-} < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{en} < \text{NO}_2^{-} < \text{CN}^{-} < \text{CO}$

Weak-field ligands are on the left, strong-field on the right.

**High spin or low spin.** Two energies compete: $\Delta_o$, the cost of promoting an electron to $e_g$, and $P$, the pairing energy, the cost of putting two electrons in one orbital.

If $\Delta_o < P$, promotion is cheaper, so electrons spread out: **high spin**, maximum unpaired electrons.

If $\Delta_o > P$, pairing is cheaper, so electrons fill $t_{2g}$ first: **low spin**, minimum unpaired electrons.

**The two iron complexes.** In both, iron is $+2$, so the configuration is $d^{6}$ in both. The metal, the oxidation state and the electron count are identical. **Only the ligand differs**, and that alone accounts for the difference.

$[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$: water is a **weak field** ligand, so $\Delta_o < P$. The electrons obey Hund's rule as far as they can, filling all five orbitals singly before pairing:

$t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$, giving **4 unpaired electrons** — **paramagnetic**.

$[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}$: cyanide is a **strong field** ligand, so $\Delta_o > P$. All six electrons pair up in the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals rather than pay the larger $\Delta_o$:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$, giving **0 unpaired electrons** — **diamagnetic**.

This pair is the cleanest possible demonstration that the ligand, not the metal, sets the magnetic behaviour — and measuring the magnetic moment is in practice how the spin state is determined.

**Why the complexes are coloured.** The gap $\Delta_o$ happens to correspond to the energy of **visible light**.

An electron in $t_{2g}$ absorbs a photon of exactly that energy and is promoted to $e_g$ — a **d-d transition**. The wavelength absorbed is removed from the white light passing through, and what we see is the **complementary colour** of what was absorbed.

Two predictions follow, and both hold:

1. A **stronger-field ligand gives a larger $\Delta_o$**, so a shorter absorbed wavelength and a different colour. $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+}$ is pale blue; adding ammonia gives the deep blue $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$.

2. An ion with **no $d$ electrons ($d^{0}$) or a full $d$ subshell ($d^{10}$) has no possible d-d transition**, and must be colourless. $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ ($d^{0}$) and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ($d^{10}$) are indeed both colourless — which is exactly what the theory requires and would be hard to explain any other way.
